name: Refugee Status Under the National Eligibility Commission (CNE) Process

requirements.blocker_text: Applicants must complete and sign the National Eligibility Commission (Commission Nationale d'Eligibilite, CNE) form, write a signed individual asylum application, and submit it with 4 passport photos to the CNE Secretariat in Dakar, followed by an interview with a CNE administrator and a second interview with a police inspector at Cite de la Police. Favorable CNE opinions are forwarded to the President of the Republic for final confirmation. The initial receipt is valid up to 6 months (renewable); a decision is expected within 4 months. Rejected applicants may appeal within 30 days to the CNE, then to the President of the Republic, or invoke a discretionary 'humanitarian option' in exceptional circumstances.
requirements.fix_path: File the asylum application with the CNE Secretariat in Dakar and attend both required interviews.

outcome.duration_length: indefinite, refugee identity card functions as a residence permit

sources.title: UNHCR Senegal -- describes the National Eligibility Commission (CNE) asylum process: application steps, dual-interview process, receipt/decision timelines, presidential confirmation of favorable opinions, and the 30-day appeal window

STATUS: DRAFT -- sourced to UNHCR's own Senegal-specific guidance (tier 2); the UNHCR page itself does not name Senegal's underlying domestic refugee statute, and this build did not independently locate/fetch the primary legislative text, so the law's name/year is not cited here. GENUINELY DISTINCTIVE PROCEDURAL FINDING: final confirmation of a favorable refugee-status decision rests with the PRESIDENT OF THE REPUBLIC personally (on CNE recommendation) -- a notably centralized, high-level confirmation step not seen in most other refugee-determination processes built in this dataset (contrast Kazakhstan's Ministry of Labor/court-appeal model or Kenya's Refugee Status Determination Committee). work_rights and study_rights set 'restricted' since the source confirms the refugee identity card functions as a residence permit but does not detail employment or education rights specifically; family_can_work left null for the same reason. Senegal has historically hosted significant Mauritanian refugee populations (from the 1989 Senegal-Mauritania border conflict) though current population figures were not independently verified in this build.
